whatWorks: The horizontal bed field itself is right, and it is the part of this that already answers the brief. Where it survives at strength -- 5658, 6051, 5789, 5003 -- the beds are flat wide rectangles at genuinely varying thickness and varying pitch, laid one over another with the dark base showing only as thin partings, and the eye reads a deposited sequence top to bottom rather than an even texture. That field is the work; everything else in the frame is currently arguing with it.

The colour relationship is already the one the direction asks for. Warm ochre and pale sand beds interrupted by desaturated cool grey beds gives the earth-over-dark reading with a cold note among the warm ones in 5003, 5789, 5920 and 6051, and the colours are held flat with no gradient anywhere in the twelve. The hues do not need reinventing; only their assignment to bed thickness does.

Seed variation is real and it varies the right quantity. Across the twelve, bed count and the evenness of bed spacing visibly differ -- 6051 carries a crowded regular section, 5396 a sparse widely-parted one -- so the primary and secondary axes of the variation strategy are already being driven by the seed rather than by colour reshuffling.

Bed count already drops under drawdown. Comparing the neutral and stress rows for 5003 and 5396, the population of fine beds visibly thins out under stress and returns in recovery, so half of the market transformation -- how many beds the section carries -- is genuinely bound and legible at 120px. Only the thickness half is running backwards.

findings.whatFails: A field of long rotated ochre slabs radiates from a pivot near the frame centre and is the loudest thing in every one of the twelve seeds. In 5265 and 5527 it is an unambiguous fan, splayed from a single point in the upper left, and the 512px single is a plume rather than a section. In 5003, 5658 and 6313 the same slabs cross the frame as a diagonal X over the beds.
findings.why: The rhythm direction says this is a stack read top to bottom and never a ring, and the focal hierarchy says nothing dominates because a section is not a scene. A radial placement asserts a centre and a scene, and it makes the diagonals the subject while the horizontal bedding becomes background texture -- the exact inversion of the intended reading.
findings.specificChange: Set the rotation of every slab in that field to zero so each one lies horizontal, and replace its radial placement with the same top-to-bottom stacking the bed field already uses: give each slab its own y position drawn from the sequence rather than an angle drawn from a centre. The slabs then become the thick beds of the section instead of a fan laid across it.
findings.keep: Keep the slabs themselves and their weight. They are the only marks in the frame carrying real thickness, and the direction wants beds that differ in thickness and weight -- so keep them as the thick members of the sequence rather than deleting them and flattening the section to one pitch.

findings.whatFails: The drawing is inset. Every seed leaves a dark margin at the left and right where the beds stop short, and most leave a substantial black band at the top or bottom -- 6444 is roughly two thirds bare base, 5265 leaves the whole lower left empty, 5920 has an empty strip along the bottom. The mass reads as a centred object sitting on black rather than as a frame cut through material.
findings.why: The composition direction says the section fills the frame edge to edge with bands running the full width and stacking from the top border to the bottom, and the density direction says the great majority of the frame carries ink with the dark base showing only as the partings. A centred mass surrounded by base makes the base the ground, which reintroduces exactly the figure-on-emptiness reading the brief refuses.
findings.specificChange: Extend every bed's horizontal extent past both frame edges -- start it left of x=0 and end it right of the frame width so no bed terminates inside the picture -- and spread the bed y positions across the full frame height from above the top border to below the bottom one, rather than clustering them about the canvas centre.
findings.keep: Keep the uneven vertical pitch. Spreading the beds to the borders must not turn into evenly distributing them: the interval between beds should still change from one part of the sequence to another, and a thick bed should still interrupt a run of thin ones.

findings.whatFails: Scattered dark brown circles sit around the drawing in 5134, 5265, 5527, 6182, 6313 and 6444, in some seeds ringing the central mass. In 6444 they form a rough halo of nine or ten discs around a small glyph, and in the 512px single they float in the empty base like bubbles.
findings.why: The motif is sediment restated as horizontal banding: wide flat marks read as a deposited sequence. A circle is neither a bed nor a parting, it has no thickness to contribute to the sequence, and a ring of them around the centre reasserts the radial composition the rhythm direction rules out. They are the clearest thing in the frame that no line of the brief asks for.
findings.specificChange: Remove the disc field entirely, and spend its ink budget on more beds -- raise the bed count by roughly the number of discs dropped. If a second primitive is needed for texture, replace the circle with a short flat rectangle of partial width, stacked with the others as a lens or a pinch-out within a bed.
findings.keep: Keep the darker umber value the discs are drawn in. It is a legitimate member of the earth palette and should reappear as the colour of some beds, so removing the discs removes a shape without narrowing the palette to ochre and grey.

findings.whatFails: In the stress row the fine beds mostly disappear and the surviving marks get visibly fatter, so stress is the heaviest, most inked, most solid state of the three. At 120px 5134 stress and 5265 stress read as near-solid ochre masses while their neutral and recovery cells read as streaked sections. Recovery is not the fullest state; stress is.
findings.why: The market transformation says the beds thin and fewer survive under drawdown, and that the sequence thickens and more beds return in recovery, so the fullest section is the recovered one. As rendered, drawdown is being drawn as consolidation into fewer heavier slabs, which is the opposite reading: a viewer would infer that stress deposits more material.
findings.specificChange: Invert the thickness response to the market sensor. Drive per-bed thickness down as drawdown deepens instead of up, so stress carries both fewer beds and thinner ones, and raise both count and thickness in recovery until total ink ordering is stress below neutral below recovery, with recovery clearly the densest of the three.
findings.keep: Keep the bed-count response, which is already correct and already legible at 120px. The count must keep falling under stress and returning in recovery; this fix changes the thickness curve only, so that both quantities move the same way instead of cancelling.

findings.whatFails: The cool grey only ever appears as the thinnest and faintest beds, sitting underneath the warm ochre mass as background texture, while the thickest marks in every seed are warm ochre. In 5265, 5527, 6182 and 6313 there is no cool bed visible at all, and the 512px single is entirely ochre and umber with no cold note anywhere.
findings.why: The focal hierarchy names the thickest cold slate band as the only local emphasis in the section, and the identity anchors require one cold band among the warm ones in every seed and every state. A cold colour applied only to the faintest marks gives the emphasis to the warm field and lets a quarter of the collection lose the palette anchor outright.
findings.specificChange: Bind the slate colour to the single thickest bed in each seed rather than to the thin ones, and add a floor of at least one slate bed per seed in every market state so it can never drop out. Make the slate a colder, bluer grey than the current neutral so it separates from the sand beds instead of reading as unsaturated ochre.
findings.keep: Keep the warm earths carrying the sequence. Umber, ochre and sand must remain the majority of the beds and the majority of the ink -- the slate is one emphatic band set among them, never a second colour family competing for the frame.

findings.whatFails: The slabs and beds are drawn semi-transparent, so wherever they cross they blend into intermediate brown and the parting between two beds is lost. The centre of 5134, 5527 and 6182 is a continuous mottled wash in which no individual bed can be traced, and pale sand beds passing under ochre slabs turn a muddy mid-tone rather than being occluded.
findings.why: The palette intent says four working colours held flat rather than graded, and the negative-space direction says the dark base surviving as partings is exactly what makes the sequence legible as distinct beds rather than as one continuous field of colour. Alpha blending manufactures a continuous gradient of unnamed intermediate colours and dissolves the partings that carry the whole reading.
findings.specificChange: Raise every bed's fill to fully opaque and let stacking order do the deposition, so a later bed occludes the one beneath it exactly as one bed of sediment covers another. Where more tonal range is wanted, add discrete darker and lighter members of umber, ochre and sand as their own flat values instead of recovering them from overlap.
findings.keep: Keep the overlap and occlusion itself. Beds crossing and cutting one another is what makes this a deposited sequence rather than a stripe pattern -- the fix is that a crossing should read as one bed covering another, not as two colours mixing.

findings.whatFails: Bedding is not merely weak in some seeds, it is essentially missing. 5527 and 6182 are a centred ochre scribble with a handful of stray ticks, 6444 is a small glyph inside a ring of discs, and 5265 carries only a short cluster of pale ticks near its centre. Four of twelve seeds do not read as a section at all at either size.
findings.why: The identity anchors require every seed and every state to keep the horizontal stacking and the full-width bedding -- that is what makes the collection one collection. A variation range whose low end reaches near-zero beds does not vary how many beds the section carries, it varies whether the piece is a section at all, and those seeds have left the brief rather than interpreted it.
findings.specificChange: Clamp the low end of the bed-count range so that no seed in any market state can fall below a section that still spans the frame -- set a floor high enough that even the sparsest seed carries beds from top border to bottom -- and bind seed variation to the spacing evenness and the thick-bed colour once the count floor is met.
findings.keep: Keep the real spread between crowded and sparse seeds. The difference between 6051's dense stack and 5396's widely-parted one is the primary variation axis the brief names, and raising the floor must not compress every seed toward the same bed count.

findings.whatFails: At 120px the fine beds break up into intermittent dashes or disappear. The pale ticks that carry 5265 at 256px are gone entirely in its 120px cell, and 5396 and 5920 lose most of their thin grey beds, leaving a centred ochre blot on black as the thumbnail reading of a piece whose 256px render is a legible section.
findings.why: The thumbnail intent requires that at 120px the work read as a stack of horizontal bands of differing thickness filling the whole frame, with the sequence legible as a sequence before any single bed can be told apart. A bed thinner than a pixel at browse size contributes nothing to that reading and its absence turns the varying pitch into noise.
findings.specificChange: Raise the minimum bed thickness to at least two pixels at 120px -- roughly 1.7 percent of frame height -- and clamp the thin end of the thickness range there, carrying the lost fine pitch instead in the parting heights, which can stay small because a dark gap between two opaque beds survives downsampling where a thin bright bed does not.
findings.keep: Keep the thickness contrast between the thinnest and thickest beds. Lifting the floor must not flatten the section toward one weight: the thick slate bed should still be several times the thinnest bed, so the eye still reads a sequence rather than a ruled grid.

overall: The bed field at the heart of this is already the right answer to the brief -- flat opaque-looking horizontal rectangles at varying thickness and varying pitch, warm earths with a cool grey among them, partings of dark base between them -- and where it runs strong, as in 5658 and 6051, the section reads exactly as intended. What is wrong is almost entirely what has been laid on top of it. A field of long rotated slabs radiates from the frame centre and dominates every seed, turning a stack into a fan and a section into a scene, and a field of dark discs rings it with a primitive the brief never asks for; between them they push the bedding into the background and leave the composition as a centred mass floating on black rather than a window cut through material. The fastest route to the brief is subtractive and reorienting rather than additive: flatten the slabs to horizontal and stack them as the thick members of the sequence, delete the discs, run every bed past both frame edges and across the full frame height, and give the cold slate to the thickest bed instead of the faintest. Two further things are running backwards rather than merely being obscured -- drawdown currently thickens the surviving marks so stress is the heaviest state when recovery should be the fullest, and the thinnest beds fall below a pixel at 120px so the browse-size reading collapses to a blot. Fix those five things and the picture that is already inside these renders is a core sample; nothing in this critique asks for a new idea, only for the one that is here to be allowed to fill the frame.
